title: Handling the mushaf
hook: many keep it high, clean, and touch it only in wudu

segments.voice: Yesterday, iltifat, who is speaking: We, I, He, and say. Your line was listen for who is speaking. Did you catch a moment when someone turned to talk to you? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Look for the Qur'an in a Muslim family's home. You probably won't find it on the floor, or under a pile of magazines, or on the bottom shelf beside the shoes. It'll be up high, often wrapped in cloth, sometimes on a shelf by itself. A grandmother may kiss it before she opens it. A child may be told never to put anything on top of it. Today: handling the mushaf.
screen: `NOT ON THE FLOOR.` → `UP HIGH, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `NOTHING ON TOP OF IT.`

segments.voice: These customs come from how Muslims regard the Qur'an: the speech of God, written down. The written copy, the mushaf, is treated with the honor due to what it carries. One rule is about touching it. Surah 56 describes the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, as a book "Which none toucheth save the purified". Scholars read that verse in more than one way. Some commentators understand it to be about the preserved book in heaven, touched only by angels. Still, the four Sunni schools of law hold, as a rule, that a person should be in a state of purity, with wudu, to touch the Arabic mushaf. They point also to a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to Yemen, recorded in the Muwatta of Imam Malik: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. Some scholars held otherwise, and there are discussions about children who are learning, about translations, and about phones and apps, which some scholars say aren't a mushaf in the same sense. Beyond the rules there's a whole culture of care. A folding wooden stand holds it open so it doesn't lie on the floor. It often sits on the highest shelf, with nothing placed on top. People avoid taking it into a bathroom. When a copy wears out, it isn't thrown in the trash: it's buried, or respectfully burned, or placed in special boxes that some mosques keep. Some Muslims kiss it; others say no such practice is required, and simply handle it with care. What the customs share is simple. This isn't an ordinary book, so it doesn't get an ordinary place.
screen: `NONE TOUCHETH SAVE THE PURIFIED` · `THE SCHOOLS: TOUCH IT WITH WUDU` · `A STAND, A HIGH SHELF, NOTHING ON TOP` · `WORN COPIES ARE BURIED, NOT TRASHED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give your copy a clean shelf. If there's a mushaf or a translation in your home, after the bell, find it a clean, high place with nothing stacked on it. For now, sit and picture where it is right now. If you don't have one, think of the one book or object in your home you treat most carefully, and why. Notice what it feels like to honor something. If you pray, you might make wudu before you next open it. The bell holds the time.
Handling the mushaf. The care Muslims give a copy of the Qur'an: purity to touch it, a high place, and never the trash. Today's word.
Your line: keep it high. Today, move one thing you value off the floor or out from under a pile, and give it a place that says it matters. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it on a high, clean shelf with nothing on top, read it on a stand, and bury or respectfully dispose of worn-out copies.

notes: Pickthall wording of 56:79 quoted from memory (it ends with a comma in Pickthall, continuing into 56:80); check.

Majority of the four Sunni schools require wudu to touch the mushaf; the Zahiri school (e.g. Ibn Hazm) and some others did not. Shi'i jurisprudence also requires purity. Confirm the 'most scholars' framing.
Phones/apps and translations: rulings vary; the script says 'many say'. Confirm.
Disposal customs (burial, burning, mosque boxes) and kissing the mushaf (some permit, some say not established): confirm.
Muwatta reference: Book 15 (the Qur'an), hadith 1, in common numbering; confirm.
